answer.rationale: The only new variable in the system is the release two hours ago; latency began climbing 30 minutes later, which is the tightest causal fit available. memory_b1 says rollback cleared a bad-build incident cleanly, and memory_b6 says this org's staged gating does surface build regressions, so a reversion is the intervention most likely to remove a cause rather than mask a symptom. But I want the archived source for memory_b1 before committing, because the summary describes an error-rate spike, not a write-latency climb, and it does not say whether that rollback happened under heavy write load — those are the two conditions that decide whether it transfers. I also want memory_b5, because routing reads off the primary is the one inherited action that directly addresses write-path latency and is far cheaper to reverse; if its source record shows it was validated at or near peak, it becomes a serious competitor and possibly the better first move given settlement traffic. Caveats I am holding: every inherited memory records a success, which is a survivorship pattern, not evidence that these actions are generally safe — the failures were likely never consolidated. Peak settlement writes make this the worst moment to roll back, since an in-flight schema or write-format change could strand or drop customer writes, which violates the primary objective more severely than elevated latency does. Confounding is real: heavy peak writes alone could produce this curve with the release entirely innocent. So I intend a guarded partial rollback on a small slice of the write fleet with write-loss instrumentation, comparing that slice against the unrolled remainder, rather than a fleet-wide reversion. If the archive shows memory_b1's rollback was error-only and untested under load, or shows memory_b5 held at peak, I will switch to routing reads to replicas as the reversible first move and hold the rollback for the next window.
